transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-11 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Navarro (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Head of ML, Mistral), Leah Ortiz (Infra Lead), Marcus Zhou (PM)

[00:00] Alex (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick round-table then we'll jump into reliability stuff. Um, Samir, Leah — want to give 30s on what you're trying to solve?
[00:12] Samir: Yeah, hi. We're Mistral Energy, uh, we run grid-alert predictions, so we have an inference pipeline that needs sub-200ms 95th percentile inside region, and when a region goes down we've had incidents where the whole pipeline degrades. Looking at Redwood to understand hosted vs dedicated vs our private option for better incident tolerance.
[00:30] Leah: We've had two outages this year with our cloud provider region — traffic failed over but latency spiked, and our alerting missed windows. So main thing is multi-region fallbacks and predictable SLOs.
[00:42] Priya (SE): Thanks, that's helpful. I'll ask a few infra questions as we go. Alex, do you want to cover how Redwood approaches multi-region routing?
[00:49] Alex: Sure. At a high level we support policy-based routing: route by latency, cost, or priority tier. For incident tolerance we recommend multi-region routing with automatic fallback to warm replicas in a secondary region. We also have configurable model-variant fallbacks — if the primary model is unavailable or under heavy load, we can route to a smaller quantized variant or to a cheaper hosted fallback.
[01:08] Samir: When you say "warm replicas" what does that mean operationally? Are they hot VMs with KV cache primed? How fast is failover?
[01:16] Priya: Great question. Warm replicas are instances kept with loaded weights and a warmed-up KV cache where feasible. Failover time depends on request routing and DNS TTLs; with our routing mesh and health checks we can fail to secondaries within 5–15s in most cases, often faster inside the same cloud provider. If you need stricter RTO we can keep cold-to-hot pre-warm pools that reduce failover to sub-5s at higher cost.
[01:41] Marcus (PM): What about stateful session/chat? Our customers use conversational context — do you preserve KV cache across failover?
[01:50] Jordan (SE): We replicate KV cache asynchronously for long-lived conversational sessions in private/dedicated setups using our cross-region KV sync; there may be a small window where you lose the most recent tokens but we can version sessions and replay last user utterances to rebuild cache quickly. For hosted we rely more on prefix caching and recommend sticky routing for sessions unless you want cross-region replication.
[02:13] Leah: Are we talking about cross-region egress charges too? Our finance team will want to see cost implications.
[02:20] Alex: Yes, cross-region traffic is billed; we include that in cost estimates. For Dedicated and Private we can place capacity in regions to reduce cross-region egress. We'll include region capacity appendix with cost sketches.
[02:33] Samir: On SLA: we have internal SLOs for the grid alerts — P99 under 400ms globally, and RTO for the inference service of under 30s for region failover. Does Redwood provide SLA numbers for Hosted? For Dedicated?
[02:45] Priya: Hosted has published availability SLAs for API endpoints — usually 99.9% depending on product tier. Dedicated offers tighter SLAs as part of reserved capacity contracts; we can do 99.95% and above with contractual terms and on-call escalation. Private deployments' SLA is more about the control plane availability versus customer-managed infra, but we offer guidance and an ops playbook.
[03:07] Samir: So 30s RTO is aggressive for a regional outage if you want full state. What are typical RTOs customers get with your multi-region config?
[03:16] Priya: Typical is 5–30s for stateless inference when there are warm replicas and routing. For stateful sessions with replication it's usually in the tens of seconds; to guarantee sub-10s with full state we'd recommend a hot-standby architecture which is possible but increases cost.
[03:33] Leah: Ok, we'd likely need a hybrid — hosted for non-critical flows, dedicated/private for the grid-alert critical pipeline. Can Redwood mix modes? Like host some routes in Redwood Hosted and pin critical models to Dedicated?
[03:44] Alex: Yes, that's a common pattern. You can route by route/model: critical route -> Dedicated in us-east + us-west warm secondaries; non-critical -> Hosted cheaper variants. The control plane is consistent so app code uses same API with routing rules.
[03:57] Marcus: About model fallbacks: how do you balance latency vs quality? If we drop to a quantized variant during failover, what's the typical quality delta?
[04:07] Priya: Quality delta depends on model family and quantization. For many recent open models a 4-bit quantized variant has minor delta for classification/alerts, but for nuanced generation there's a bigger gap. We run evals per workload and can surface regression thresholds. You can also configure a policy: only fallback for requests where confidence is high or for certain endpoints.
[04:25] Samir: That per-request policy is interesting. Our alerting pipeline has a confidence score attached; could you make routing decisions based on inference confidence?
[04:33] Jordan: Yes — routing can be conditional on request metadata. E.g., if confidence < threshold, route to a higher-fidelity model or mark for human review. Those policies are part of our route configuration.
[04:45] Leah: Security — for Private deployment we need KMS/HSM integration and audit logs. Does Redwood support customer-managed KMS and SSO?
[04:54] Alex: Yes. For Private and Dedicated we support customer KMS (AWS KMS cross-account, GCP CMEK) and HSM integrations. We also provide audit logging, and we support SAML/SSO + SCIM for user provisioning. We'll attach our SOC2 controls and sample audit logs.
[05:10] Samir: Any concerns about data residency? We need EU data to stay in EU region for some customers.
[05:17] Priya: We offer region pinning and residency controls. For Hosted we have region options and will keep data in-region; Dedicated/Private gives you full control. We'll include region-specific controls in the appendix.
[05:29] Marcus: Can we run a quick example of what's involved in a canary/rollback? We want automated rollback if latency regresses beyond X% in 15 minutes.
[05:38] Jordan: Rollouts support health checks, canary percentages, and automatic rollback triggers by latency, error rate, or custom metrics. You can define a 15-minute window and a 10% P95 latency threshold; if breached, the system automatically rolls back and alerts.
[05:54] Leah: Who's on-call on Redwood side for Dedicated incidents? We need a contact and escalation path in contract.
[06:01] Alex: For Dedicated we provide 24/7 support for critical incidents depending on SLA tier, with escalation to our infra/SE on-call. We'll put escalation contacts in the SLA matrix.
[06:10] Samir: About observability — we need token-level latency breakdowns tied to routes and models, and traces that join our request IDs with Redwood. Does that exist?
[06:18] Priya: Yes. We emit per-request traces and we can ingest customer-supplied request IDs to correlate. Token-level cost and latency breakdowns are in Redwood Console; you can set alerts and export metrics via Prometheus or our API.
[06:33] Marcus: What about benchmarking? We want to run a smoke benchmark with our sample payloads and compare Hosted baseline vs Dedicated. How long does that take and what data do you need?
[06:42] Jordan: Usually we run short smoke tests (an hour) for throughput and latency at representative QPS. We'll need sample request payloads and expected concurrency; we'll share a script and a results sheet. For Dedicated we'd run on reserved capacity or simulate similar CPU/GPU profiles.
[06:56] Samir: Ok that sounds good. Our P99 requirements are strict. We'll share the P99/P95 tables and typical concurrency.
[07:04] Leah: One more on failover: if a region is degraded but not fully down, do you do gradient-weighted routing? Like shift traffic gradually to avoid overload on secondaries.
[07:15] Priya: Yes, we support gradual shift and custom weight schedules. You can also configure automatic throttling and circuit breakers to prevent collapse.
[07:26] Alex: Quick note — in our experience customers implement multi-region with sticky sessions for conversational flows and cross-region replication for critical state; the rest of traffic uses cheaper fallbacks.
[07:37] Samir: Budget question — keeping warm replicas in two regions doubles baseline cost roughly. What levers do we have to optimize cost?
[07:45] Alex: Levers: adaptive pre-warm pools (scaleers based on traffic patterns), mixed model families (smaller cheaper variants for non-critical), prefix caching, and auto-batching for throughput. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization and batching settings by workload.
[07:59] Marcus: Let's discuss timeline — we want a pilot in Q1. Is that realistic?
[08:03] Alex: Yes, pilot in Q1 is realistic. Pilot typically includes a small dedicated cluster or private deployment for critical route, plus benchmarking and runbook validation.
[08:12] Samir: Good. For procurement: what docs will you need? Security questionnaire, contract draft, and pricing.
[08:19] Alex: We'll send SOC2, security questionnaire answers, and a draft MSA for Dedicated. Pricing depends on committed capacity for Dedicated and region placement; we'll include Hosted pricing for fallback routes.
[08:29] Leah: For the Private option, network-wise we'll need to map peering/VPN options.
[08:33] Priya: We'll coordinate with your network team; Jordan will follow up.
[08:38] Alex: Ok wrapping up. Recap and owners: we'll send SLA matrix, region appendix, SOC2, and a sample incident runbook. Priya will prepare fallback config examples. Samir and Leah will share latency tables and infra diagrams.
[08:55] Marcus: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[09:00] Alex: Thanks — we'll follow up with a calendar to set the scoping call.
